items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

Continue reading...
items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

items.title: Was Heineken’s ‘Pub Succession’ the most successful ad campaign ever to fail?
items.summary:
On Achill Island off Ireland’s west coast, there’s a pub that’s been in the McLoughlin family since 1870. Its owner, the fourth-generation publican Josie McLoughlin, was ready to retire but had no one in the family willing to take over. All he wanted was another McLoughlin to keep the pub running and the name above the door. 

So Heineken stepped in and launched a global search for a successor. Ads from Times Square to Sydney. Press coverage in 128 countries. More than 2,000 people responded. Heineken flew two McLoughlin descendants to Ireland to meet Josie.

The campaign, “Pub Succession,” won five Cannes Lions in 2025 and made the shortlist for the festival’s top prize. In 2026, it added three D&AD Pencils and a Clio Grand . By every ad industry measure, it was a hit.

The problem? The campaign didn’t work.

McLoughlin’s closed on September 27. Nobody took over. It’s still for sale for 550,000 euros ($605,000), the same price at which it was listed for nearly two years before Heineken stepped in. Whoever succeeded Josie was always going to have to buy the pub.

Heineken says brokering a deal was never its job. Its role, a spokesperson says, was to “help McLoughlin’s identify potential successors, not to manage the sale.” Besides, the company adds, Irish law states that only licensed real estate agents can broker a sale. Fair enough. But Heineken wrote the pitch, and the pitch wasn’t just about introductions. It was about finding the next McLoughlin.

Why 2,000 sign-ups weren’t enough 

The pubs you’re probably picturing are your local American iterations of Irish pubs or…
items.t: Was Heineken’s ‘Pub Succession’ the most successful ad campaign ever to fail?

items.title: How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy
items.summary:
Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.

Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may no longer need to work. Indeed, studies show that employees at post-IPO companies are more likely to leave their jobs or become less satisfied .

Management experts and executives who have successfully navigated IPOs say there are a few ways companies can make sure that doesn’t happen.

GIVE EMPLOYEES A REASON TO WORK OTHER THAN MONEY 

The most important thing is to make sure workers have a sense of purpose that goes beyond making money, something Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin highlighted explicitly in a letter to prospective shareholders when the company went public in 2004.

“Talented people are attracted to Google because we empower them to change the world,” they wrote. “We are focused on providing an environment where talented, hardworking people are rewarded for their contributions to Google and for making the world a better place.”

Laszlo Bock, who oversaw Google’s human resources operations for a decade following its IPO, echoed that sentiment nearly 10 years later .

“We spend more time working than we do on almost any other activity in our lives,” he wrote. “People want all that time to mean something.”

Of course, it is ideal if that sense of purpose is already in place before a company goes public.

“If a company’s employees are coming to work just to…
items.t: How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy

items.title: Young people may be holding back gender equality at work
items.summary:
About two decades ago, a substantial body of academic research started to provide evidence for what many had long suspected: Young people were leading the way toward a more gender-equal world.

European Social Survey data from 2004 and 2010 found that younger adults were considerably less likely than their older counterparts to endorse traditional gender roles. In 2009, Pew Research found that Americans under the age of 30 were considerably more liberal in their attitudes toward women’s roles than older generations. And in 2015, a study published in Psychology of Women Quarterly found that millennials held more egalitarian attitudes toward women’s work and family roles than baby boomers had at the same age.

The direction of travel seemed clear: Each new generation was broadly more supportive of gender equality than the last.

Over the last few years, though, there’s been a disconcerting shift. In several recent surveys, young men—and in some cases young women—have expressed more traditional attitudes toward gender roles, and greater skepticism about efforts to advance women’s equality, than men old enough to be their fathers or grandfathers.

And there’s evidence that this generational divide extends to attitudes toward leadership, too. This month, the Reykjavík Index for Leadership —an annual study conducted by global research firm Verian and the Reykjavík Global Foundation, an Iceland-based nonprofit—found that younger adults are considerably less likely than their older counterparts to believe women and men are equally suited to lead.

items.t: Young people may be holding back gender equality at work

items.title: Have you ever been told that there was something about you that was ‘too much’?
items.summary:
Inflection points spark reflection. And currently, I’m at two inflection points: approaching 10 years of being in business and the end of another calendar year. One of the things I am recalling is that as a woman, some of my characteristics that I once thought of as deficits have conspired to be my greatest assets. Unbeknownst to me, they are actually the factors that contribute to my success.

For example, I am indecisive. I constantly weigh the pros and cons of a situation . I blame that in part on being a Libra — but that trait is also why I loved studying cultural anthropology and gravitate towards multidisciplinary work. In my job history I was sometimes told that I had to “pick a lane.. And it’s been brought to my attention multiple times, especially in corporate environments, that decisiveness is a winning attribute. But as I have evolved, my indecisiveness is the very quality that helps me consider multiple perspectives and identify alternative future scenarios of a situation. Ironically, my indecisiveness helps me navigate ambiguous terrain. 

How wonderful that years later that ability to straddle lanes and work in multidisciplinary environments has become my asset as I’ve built a company to help people toggle between wonder and rigor. 

What about others? 

I was curious to learn from other women if an inherent quality that they were told was “too much” turned out to be a creative asset in their work. Bear with me — I know that such a question could be posed to men too. But in my experience, it’s women who tend to contort themselves in order to fit into the…
items.t: Have you ever been told that there was something about you that was ‘too much’?

items.title: I coach four-time Grand Slam champion Aryna Sabalenka. Here’s why winners shouldn’t always focus on speed
items.summary:
For years, I was always a step behind on the jujitsu mat. I’d rush, scramble, and attack from poor positions. I was reacting to my opponent’s game plan, not mine. In the end, I was defeated.

Then one day, time slowed down. I was present, maybe even a little ahead of the moment. My partner was relentless in his attack, but I wasn’t chasing him. My heart rate and breathing settled. When he moved, I was a step ahead. 

The first thing you learn on the mat isn’t how to win. It’s how to defend.

That moment was a result of years of drilling defense. It provided me room to breathe, adapt, and attack based on MY game plan.

Jujitsu changed forever for me that day. 

My coach, Jhunior Guarnido, teaches it as a process: Defend, Control, Attack. 

It starts as a sequence you cycle through, but as you improve, it becomes one continuous forward motion. Defense and Control are built into the Attack. You want to act without hesitation, but never lead by pure emotion, reckless behavior, or your opponent’s timeline.

Defend, Control, Attack gives you the freedom to play to win. If the Attack isn’t going to plan, you flow through the sequence and begin again. This is how winners operate.

I’ve coached Aryna Sabalenka for eight years but also work with founders and executives. When they’ve felt pressure, most go straight into an attack. I love that. Wanting to dictate the pace and outcome is what winners do.

The problem is their awareness and timing. Before you see what’s really happening, you move from a bad position, often from fear or a forced reaction on a clock someone else set.

items.t: I coach four-time Grand Slam champion Aryna Sabalenka. Here’s why winners shouldn’t always focus on speed

items.title: America is in a turkey slump
items.summary:
One of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast . While that remains the norm , Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared.

I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays . I find turkeys fascinating , because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard.

And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump.

Receding since the late 1990s 

Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business.

More than $5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed.

However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds.

While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway . Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline.

It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds in 1995 to 104 pounds in 2025.

items.t: America is in a turkey slump

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org
items.t: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras

items.title: ‘Millennials need to retire,’ say frustrated Gen Z job seekers on TikTok
items.summary:
Millennials need to retire. That’s the sentiment in certain corners of TikTok , where some Gen Zers struggling to find jobs are blaming the generation directly above them for their inability to get a foot on the corporate ladder. 

The problem is that millennials are only in their thirties and forties and not even close to retiring. And they don’t have anything to do with Gen Z’s struggles anyway.

A few videos have been doing the rounds in which Zoomers complain about their lack of job prospects. In one from earlier this year , a creator argued that millennials “monopolize the job market” because they know Gen Zers would surpass them if they were given the same opportunities. 

Another lamented , “millennials are taking all the jobs that we went to school for,” claiming that Gen Zers, meanwhile, have to take lower-paying jobs in retail and fast-food restaurants. Others angrily suggest millennials “retire” so Gen Z can take the jobs for themselves.

Gen Z’s frustrations are valid. They have plenty to be worried about, from an entry-level job crisis to the AI boom . But none of this is millennials’ fault. 

Born between 1981 and 1996, many millennials were graduating college just after the 2008 financial crisis. Some entered a job market with few opportunities, and later experienced layoffs or had to pivot careers as industries were disrupted. 

Fast-forward to now, and many are dealing with yet another period of economic instability while trying to manage the financial pressures of housing, bills, children, and aging parents.

Plenty of workers would gladly retire if they…
items.t: ‘Millennials need to retire,’ say frustrated Gen Z job seekers on TikTok

items.title: 4 places where cutting AI costs is a mistake
items.summary:
Every leader says the same thing when they roll out a new AI tool. “Give it to our employees, let them run!” What actually happens three months later is that access gets capped, usage gets metered, and exploration gets restricted to the people with the most seniority.

What happened? A scarcity mindset took hold, driven by the assumption that controlling costs means restricting employees’ access to tools.

Here are the four places a scarcity mindset shows up most frequently, and what you can do about it.

1. Metering access like a utility bill 

Companies like Tesla, Uber, and Meta have started to cap spending . Tesla, for example, now limits employees to $200 per week. On paper, that sounds reasonable. But for developers who have built these tools into their daily work, hitting the limit doesn’t magically make their deadlines or responsibilities disappear.

Instead, developers are forced to make a decision. Do they use the assistance now to improve their work, or save it for a harder assignment later? This kind of metering is the equivalent of telling employees that their laptop batteries last just one hour and can be charged only once a day.

The far better way to control costs is to match the tool to the task. While it’s easy to reach for the most powerful model every single time, think of it like renting a car for your next trip to the grocery store. A Ferrari costs far more than a Toyota, and doesn’t make any material difference in terms of getting your groceries home. Likewise, a routine coding task doesn’t need the most expensive artificial intelligence model to…
items.t: 4 places where cutting AI costs is a mistake

items.title: ‘No one asked for this’: AI is being pushed on people—and they’re sick of it
items.summary:
The AI era is fully here—and while companies bill it as a solution to problems, consequences like mass layoffs , environmental effects , privacy concerns , and the slopification of culture have many people fed up with something they never wanted in the first place.

The technology faces growing resentment from workers, who are being urged to embrace AI tools even as businesses have rushed to reduce their workforces in favor of automation. 

Online, many posts about AI capture a growing frustration with how these tools—and their disruptions—are being forced on users.

“Nobody asked for Google to be worse—but AI made it happen,” one X user recently remarked . “No one asked for computer hardware costs to rise—but AI made it happen. No one asked for human customer service to be replaced—but AI made it happen.”

In another post , Sarah Hoyt, a science fiction, fantasy, and mystery author, said she doesn’t hate artificial intelligence, but is “begging all the crazy people out there to stop pushing AI where no one asked for it.”

The disenchantment plays out in the data: In 2019, 81% of Glassdoor reviews mentioning AI were positive, the company said , compared with 43% this year. Meanwhile, Pew Research found that 52% of Americans were more concerned than excited about AI, up from 37% in 2021. And in an Ipsos poll from June, 67% of respondents thought AI would worsen the worker experience.

“The closest analog is the replacement of physical labor throughout the long Industrial Revolution,” said Jiemin Tina Wei, an assistant professor of history at Florida International…
items.t: ‘No one asked for this’: AI is being pushed on people—and they’re sick of it

items.title: Marc Andreessen has a surprisingly mundane prediction about AI’s impact
items.summary:
When it comes to AI ’s potential impact on the economy, Marc Andreessen thinks extreme optimists and extreme pessimists have one thing in common: they are both wrong. 

“Both the utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed [by] the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact [of AI], and specifically the economic impact,” the prominent venture capitalist said Monday at the Federal Reserve’s AI conference in San Francisco.

Andreessen thinks both camps are overlooking that vast economic sectors—including health care, education, housing, law, and government—are blocked from rapid transformation by heavy regulation, limited competition, and other factors.

While this could limit AI-driven job losses in those sectors, it could also make their services increasingly expensive relative to other goods and services.

“[Health care] is already a fifth of U.S. GDP, and I don’t see why it doesn’t go to a fourth, a third and then half and then ultimately 80%,” Andreessen said.

The implications of this view depend on your values, he added. 

“You might interpret this as good news, because it means the AI revolution is not going to, you know, destroy all the jobs or kill everybody,” he said. “You could also view this as very negative, which is [that] productivity … simply may not grow very much.”

Andreessen is the co-founder and general partner of Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force.

Andreessen’s comments on Monday marked a change in tone, if not substance, from many of his…
items.t: Marc Andreessen has a surprisingly mundane prediction about AI’s impact

items.title: The price of success nobody warns founders about: Who are you after you sell your company?
items.summary:
We entrepreneurs spend decades learning how to build, scale, and exit successful businesses, and there are countless books, podcasts, courses, and articles dedicated to the pursuit of this goal.

Yet almost nobody teaches us how to live after the exit.

In 2008, I did what most entrepreneurs dream of doing. I exited the business I’d spent nearly two decades building, just before the global financial crisis. By almost any measure, it was a remarkable success.

What I discovered, and what I want to share with my fellow entrepreneurs, is that no one tells you about the psychological consequences of success. We celebrate the exit as the ultimate achievement: the culmination of years of sacrifice, sleepless nights, and relentless determination. A liquidity event takes place and the founder collects the check and disappears into a life of freedom and fulfilment. That’s the narrative, anyway.

But my experience was very different, because my identity was fully linked to my business and everything it represented. I didn’t recognize it then, but I’d confused what I did with who I was. Without the business, I wasn’t entirely sure who I was anymore, and almost overnight my identity disappeared.

What I’ve come to find out is that this is much more common than you may think it is.

The hidden cost of no exit plan 

I built my property advisory business, Ober-Haus, after arriving in Estonia in the early 1990s, and developed it into a company that operated across seven countries. For nearly 20 years, my life revolved around building, negotiating, financing, and solving problems. I loved…
items.t: The price of success nobody warns founders about: Who are you after you sell your company?

items.title: How the Supreme Court’s college admissions decision has changed the job pipeline for Black and Latino students
items.summary:
Jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce.

They interviewed juniors for internships that often led to full-time offers. Finance firms came and ran affinity information sessions and job shadowing programs for first- and second-year students.

“They would specifically say: ‘We’re looking for BIPOC students. We’re looking for first-gen students. We’re looking for LGBTQIA+ students,’” said Chambers, executive director of the school’s Hameetman Career Center.

Not anymore. Those pipelines, Chambers said, have “dried up.” 

After a divided Supreme Court gutted race-conscious admissions in 2023, colleges could no longer give an edge to Black and Latino applicants over white and Asian applicants in the name of diversity, ushering in a new era for higher education. That meant the end of policies aimed at turning around historically low representation and systemic discrimination. 

The court’s ruling —which more than two-thirds of American adults told Gallup was “mostly a good thing”—did not address or change hiring laws nor mention employer efforts to make workplaces more inclusive.

Yet many employers have since dismantled existing efforts to recruit diverse workers on college campuses, reporting by The Hechinger Report and Soledad O’Brien Productions found. 

Company leaders removed or revised diversity language, changed recruitment strategies and reconsidered how they built pools of candidates, according to a Columbia Business School study based on a survey of human resources…
items.t: How the Supreme Court’s college admissions decision has changed the job pipeline for Black and Latino students

items.title: How to clock out psychologically—and leave the bad vibes at work
items.summary:
It’s hard to leave work stress where it belongs: at work. 

Stressful days spent navigating tense conversations with coworkers or clients, or staring down an endless to-do list or email queue, can cause rumination, anxiety, and even after-hours work. Your job anxiety can easily, and frequently, spill into your personal life.

To break the cycle, experts suggest creating a wind-down routine.

Understanding Emotional Residue and Rumination 

Our brains are hardwired to replay unfinished business, which is why you can’t just turn off your thoughts after a tough day at work. Forcing yourself to stop thinking about a stressful situation usually backfires, and this can exacerbate your worry. 

“Trying not to think about it, generally does not work, as our brains will latch harder onto anything we’re trying to push out,” notes psychologist Meera Khan, clinical director at the mental health treatment company LifeStance Health in Bensalem, Pennsylvania.

Without a solid routine to wrap up your workday, spillover stress easily creeps into dinner time and ruins the rest of your night, according to the Journal of Occupational Health Psychology .

“When something upsetting happens at work, the stress doesn’t automatically disappear just because the workday is over,” explains neuropsychologist Sanam Hafeez, director of the neuropsychological assessment practice Comprehend the Mind in New York. “Your mind will oftentimes replay the moment over and over, trying to make sense of what happened,” she says. 

To break free from that mental loop, research published in the journal Acta…
items.t: How to clock out psychologically—and leave the bad vibes at work

items.title: A new report says free childcare in NYC will pay for itself
items.summary:
Since taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made it his mission to expand access to affordable childcare in the city, and for good reason. On average, NYC families spend $21,000 on childcare annually per child—equaling an estimated $10 billion citywide every year. While about 40% of children in the city receive some free or subsidized care, the remaining 60% receive none, leaving many families to pay entirely out of pocket.

A new report reveals how universal childcare would not only benefit families in New York City, but also boost the economy: Just 35 hours of free childcare per week could bring up to $6.5 billion in economic value each year, which would likely exceed the cost of providing that care. 

The report—which was produced by a nonpartisan think tank, the 5BORO Institute at Citizens Union, in partnership with Boston Consulting Group—surveyed more than 2,700 parents of children younger than 5, along with about a hundred families who moved away from New York City recently. 

According to the report, nearly 70% of children under the age of 6 are cared for by parents or adults who work. When those parents are unable to find care and forced to drop out of the workforce or switch jobs, the city loses $1.7 billion in annual income; among the parents surveyed, 15% altered their work situation due to childcare issues. For hourly workers, childcare gaps can force them to miss out on $360 million in earnings each year. The report also found that childcare was a leading concern for families who had left the city, a growing trend that is supported by plenty…
items.t: A new report says free childcare in NYC will pay for itself

items.title: All these outages show how corporate America needs to modernize out-of-date tech
items.summary:
Over the past five days, a string of high-profile tech outages has left Americans struggling to send emails, catch flights, and access their bank accounts.

While the disruptions raised concerns about AI -powered cybersecurity threats, the real culprit may be something less sinister: corporate America’s tech systems are simply out of date. 

Outages like those at JPMorgan Chase , the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , and Microsoft can occur when computer systems are undergoing major upgrades, Marva Bailer, CEO of tech advisory firm Qualaix, told the New York Post . Bolting on new technology can leave the systems vulnerable.

Although it is unclear whether the recent outages were directly related to artificial intelligence, many organizations are currently upgrading their networks to handle AI tools. Microsoft attributed its outage to an issue that arose during a network capacity upgrade, according to the Financial Times . 

The time of year could also be a factor, as technicians rush to make sure systems are ready for the holiday shopping and travel season.

“It’s holiday time, it’s travel time, it’s shopping,” Bailer told the New York Post . “So, you have all those higher spikes in volume and more pressure to [update your systems].”

AI is also allowing companies to identify software vulnerabilities far more quickly, possibly leaving IT workers with too much work on their hands, the Post reported.

Like Bailer, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the disruptions to companies trying to upgrade aging systems, during an appearance on CNBC…
items.t: All these outages show how corporate America needs to modernize out-of-date tech

items.title: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy feared being ‘a lousy dad’—so he did this
items.summary:
When Amazon CEO Andy Jassy became a parent for the first time 26 years ago, he didn’t want to choose between being a good worker and being a good father.

That left him with only one option.

“I realized that I had to change the way I worked,” Jassy recently said during an appearance at Amazon’s Bring Your Parents to Work Day. “[Otherwise,] I was either going to have to leave Amazon, or I was going to be a lousy dad.”

Jassy was used to working grueling hours—often staying at the office late into the night —and he wasn’t sure if he could do his job effectively on a tighter schedule.

“I didn’t know how I would do my job without [working all the time],” he said. “But like everything else, if you think about it and you rework it and you find ways to be more efficient and you make trade-offs, you can do it.”

One step was to ensure that, whenever he was at the office, he was using his time efficiently.

“I did spend a lot of time in the hallway talking to people, and I wasn’t always prioritizing the things that mattered most,” Jassy said. “It forced me to get more efficient in what I did.”

He also established rules to help him prioritize family: being home for dinner every day, having weekly breakfasts with each of his children, and maintaining a standing Tuesday date night with his wife.

The challenge Jassy faced will likely be familiar to any parent struggling to balance career ambitions with responsibilities at home. And it is increasingly common among men, a growing number of whom say they are interested in being parents or caregivers.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: Slack and Teams have a neurotypical bias. Here’s how to fix it
items.summary:
Text-based workplace communication platforms like Slack, Teams and email can create challenges for neurodiverse workers. But most have easy fixes—and the solutions can benefit all workers.

According to an analysis by BRYGE AI , an online tool that helps make messages more neurodiverse friendly, most workers fail to recognize the ways in which their communication style poses challenges for recipients with autism, ADHD, dyslexia, or other neurological or learning differences. 

For example, research suggests that it takes most people an average of over 23 minutes to return to a task after being interrupted, and that workers are interrupted every two minutes by an email, meeting or notification. Getting back on track, however, can be especially difficult for those with ADHD, who often struggle with task paralysis , executive dysfunction and a more fragile working memory.

“Slack and Teams have the green dot, there are typing bubbles, read receipts, received and sent signals, all built into it—so now, there’s an implicit pressure to respond right away,” explains BRYGE AI founder and AI engineering lead for Uptrend Motion, Rebecca Koniahgari. “We took these flexible tools and turned them into a stopwatch, where everybody is being judged by visibility.”

Working across communication channels can also make it hard for anyone—but especially neurodiverse workers—to find a needle in a haystack of information. When answers are not easy to find, or when requests are not made explicit, those with autism or ADHD can quickly become overwhelmed.

items.title: This is the wrong reason to claim Social Security benefits early
items.summary:
YouTube creator Erin Moriarity recently appeared on Morningstar’s The Long View podcast. She spoke with podcast hosts Christine Benz and Amy Arnott about why she feels positive about the future of Social Security benefits ; her advice for young people planning for retirement; and Social Security mistakes to watch out for.

You like to push back on concerns about the future of Social Security. Can you explain why you think that people who are, say, over 50 should feel some comfort that their promised benefits will be there for them? 

MORIARITY: People over 50 vote, and those in Congress know it. If they upset that population, it’s not going to go well for them. They’re going to lose their job. I think Congress has a huge motivation to act. I do think Social Security will experience reform and will see changes. I don’t necessarily know what those changes would be, whether it’s reducing cost-of-living adjustments going forward, increasing the wage cap. I mean, there might be the potential that they try to borrow in order to fund the trust fund, which we’ve never done before. They would have to rewrite the laws, but there’s going to be a way in which they keep Social Security going forward. And I think people over 50 don’t have to worry about changes to their benefits. I think people in my generation, 30s, I think benefits will change, but benefits will be there.

items.title: Tuesday briefing: Andy Burnham’s government wants to get young people into work. Will cutting their benefits help?

Good morning. The former health secretary, Alan Milburn, will publish his long-awaited review into the one million young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) later today. The report will propose cutting welfare for some under-25s and spending billions on a new “deal” for young people. The government is at pains to tell you that its approach to welfare is nothing like that of the Tories’: Labour isn’t the party of “crude” benefit cuts, and it sees youth worklessness as a “moral” issue for which young people aren’t to blame.

It’s hard to recall a government report more heavily trailed than this one. items.title: Why Alan Milburn’s Pip plan is a mistake | Letters
items.summary:
Savitri Hensman says financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest

Alan Milburn has a track record of so-called cost-cutting measures that waste billions of pounds in public money while making health worse. The private finance initiative was an expensive mess, though it did help huge companies and rich people get richer. It is less surprising that he wants more benefits for young sick and disabled people slashed than that the government might go along with this (Some young disabled people to lose Pip in Milburn plan – but can apply to local fund, 12 November).

Financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest. The high number of young people not in education, employment or training is probably largely due to past top-level decisions. Austerity, making life tougher for claimants while favouring multimillionaires, fewer youth clubs, underfunded mental health care, long delays in providing assessments and equipment, and making school and university more stressful have not only caused suffering but also been expensive.
